s1: The CFH Y402H variant fails to restrain intracellular alternative-pathway C3 tickover in RPE endolysosomes, causing C3b opsonization of organelles and C5AR1 signaling that blocks autophagy completion and sensitizes RPE cells to C5b-9-mediated lysis.
s2: A surface-seeking complement factor H biologic restores alternative-pathway control at the heparan sulfate-rich Bruch's membrane, decaying C3bBb convertases and limiting C3b/C5b-9 deposition on RPE and choriocapillaris despite CFB and C3 risk-variant-driven amplification.

s1: Reactive astrocytes and microglia downregulate SLC1A2 (EAAT2/GLT-1), reducing synaptic glutamate clearance and elevating extracellular glutamate to drive Ca2+-dependent excitotoxic motor neuron death through AMPA and NMDA receptors.
s2: Astrocyte-targeted gene delivery restores EAAT2/GLT-1 transporter density at perisynaptic astrocytic processes, normalizing extracellular glutamate and aborting Ca2+-dependent excitotoxic motor neuron injury.

s1: Age- and genotype-driven loss of CFH regulation on Bruch's membrane permits unchecked CFB-stabilized alternative-pathway C3 convertase activity, causing C3b/iC3b deposition and C5b-9 formation on RPE cells that drives complement-dependent RPE death and centrifugal enlargement of geographic atrophy.
s2: Inactivate complement factor B (block its Ba-mediated binding to C3b or its serine-protease Bb function) so the alternative-pathway C3 convertase cannot form or persist, thereby restoring effective convertase control that the aged/risk-genotype CFH haplotype fails to provide.

s1: Oxidative glycation strips GPI-anchored CD59 from the RPE surface, removing the final checkpoint on terminal complement and permitting repeated sublytic C5b-9 and poly-C9 insertion that causes calcium influx, NFKB1 activation, and apoptotic RPE loss.
s2: Activate GLO1-mediated carbonyl detoxification in RPE to retain and restore endogenous surface CD59 rather than broadly suppressing proximal complement.

s1: Misfolded SOD1 (e.g., D90A, G93A) acts as a self-templating seed that catalyzes conformational conversion of native SOD1 into aggregation-prone conformers, so stabilizing the SOD1 dimer interface with NABi-like inhibitors will block seeded propagation and slow motor neuron loss.
s2: Misfolded SOD1 conformers (e.g., D90A, G93A) self-template conversion of native SOD1 into aggregation-prone monomers; small-molecule stabilization of the SOD1 dimer interface prevents monomer release and seed-catalyzed conformational conversion.

s1: TDP-43 downregulation represses ADARB1 (ADAR2) expression, causing failure of Q/R site editing in GRIA2 (GluA2) AMPA receptor subunits, yielding calcium-permeable AMPA receptors that drive excitotoxic Ca2+ overload and downstream mitochondrial and ER stress specifically in motor neurons.
s2: Astrocyte-targeted gene delivery restores EAAT2/GLT-1 transporter density at perisynaptic astrocytic processes, normalizing extracellular glutamate and aborting Ca2+-dependent excitotoxic motor neuron injury.

s1: Photooxidative lysosomal membrane permeabilization releases CTSB while drusen-borne amyloid-beta oligomers, oxidized lipids, and C1Q prime NLRP3, together driving CASP1-dependent maturation of IL1B and IL18 and GSDMD-mediated pyroptotic RPE death at focal atrophy sites.
s2: Readouts include GSDMD cleavage/oligomerization, propidium iodide uptake, LDH release, IL1B/IL18 release, transepithelial resistance, and en-face RPE lesion expansion.

s1: Repeat-associated non-AUG translation of the C9orf72 expansion produces arginine-rich dipeptide repeat proteins (poly-GR, poly-PR) that enter nucleoli, disrupt NPM1-dependent ribosome biogenesis, and stabilize TP53, driving motor neuron death.
s2: Readouts: immunofluorescence for NPM1 nucleolar localization, 5-ethynyl uridine incorporation to measure rRNA transcription/processing, nucleolar stress markers (nucleolin relocalization), TP53 protein levels, and motor neuron survival under chronic DPR burden.

s1: Stressed RPE sheds exosomes enriched in complement C3 and miR-155 with reduced miR-146a, whose uptake by choroidal macrophages and endothelium represses SOCS1 and unleashes IRAK1/NFKB signaling, boosting macrophage TNF/IL6 output that feeds back onto RPE.
s2: Blocking C3 cleavage intracellularly cuts the cascade upstream of both C3b opsonization and C5b-9 formation, and clinical slowing of GA by extracellular C3 inhibition (pegcetacoplan) validates the node while leaving the intracellular compartment unaddressed.

s1: The GGGGCC repeat expansion at C9ORF72 produces RNA foci and RAN-translated dipeptide repeat proteins (poly-GR, poly-GA) that bind karyopherin KPNB1 and nucleoporin NUP62, inhibiting TNPO1-dependent import and collapsing the Ran gradient, thereby causing nucleocytoplasmic transport failure and cytoplasmic accumulation of TDP-43 and FUS.
s2: Inhibit accumulation and repeat-associated non-AUG translation of the pathogenic expanded transcript while preserving sufficient C9orf72 haploexpression, thereby restoring nucleocytoplasmic transport.

s1: Age-related MTORC1 hyperactivation and declining ATP6V0A1-dependent V-ATPase activity alkalinize RPE lysosomes, reducing CTSD activity and retaining TFEB in the cytosol, collapsing autophagic flux with SQSTM1 accumulation, impaired photoreceptor outer-segment digestion, lipofuscin buildup, and lysosomal membrane permeabilization.
s2: Readouts include rescue of autophagic flux (LC3-II and SQSTM1 turnover with lysosomal blockade), reduced C5AR1 activation, and improved cell survival upon human serum complement challenge.

s1: Drusen-borne DAMPs (amyloid-beta oligomers, A2E) and photooxidized bisretinoid/lysosomal rupture products prime RPE through TLR4-MYD88 and license the NLRP3-PYCARD inflammasome, so that CASP1-mediated maturation of IL1B/IL18 and GSDMD-dependent pyroptotic lysis releases further DAMPs that propagate paracrine inflammation and RPE monolayer collapse at the GA margin.
s2: NLRP3 is the convergence point for both the TLR4-MYD88 priming signal (pro-IL1B/pro-IL18 transcription) and the lysosomal-rupture/photooxidized-bisretinoid activation signal, so its inhibition simultaneously blocks cytokine maturation and GSDMD-mediated pyroptotic DAMP release.

s1: Cytosolic DNA from leaky mitochondria or reverse-transcribed retroelements activates the CGAS-STING1-TBK1-IRF3 axis in RPE, producing chronic type I interferon (IFNB1) and CXCL10 that recruit CXCR3+ cytotoxic CD8 T cells and NK cells to form a cytotoxic front enlarging the atrophic lesion.
s2: Hit criteria: >=30% reduction in lesion expansion and CXCL10 with preserved ERG a/b waves.

s1: Progressive depletion of nuclear TDP-43 (TARDBP) derepresses cryptic exon insertion into STMN2 and UNC13A pre-mRNAs, reducing functional stathmin-2 and MUNC13A protein and driving distal axon degeneration of motor neurons.
s2: Cytoplasmic TDP-43 sequestration of RMDN3 weakens the VAPB-RMDN3 ER-mitochondria tether, collapsing ITPR1-VDAC1 calcium transfer and ATP production in motor neurons.

s1: Oxidative nitration-mediated loss of membrane-bound CD59 on RPE cells permits persistent sublytic C5b-9 insertion, driving Ca2+ influx, arachidonic-acid release, and an IL6/CXCL8 secretory state that culminates in RPE apoptosis and choriocapillaris injury.
s2: Key readouts include reduced C5b-9 deposition (immunocytochemistry for MAC), decreased Fluo-4-measured Ca2+ flux, suppression of IL6/CXCL8 secretion by ELISA, and improved RPE monolayer integrity (TEER, ZO-1 staining).

s1: Oxidative glycation strips GPI-anchored CD59 from the RPE surface, removing the final checkpoint on terminal complement and permitting repeated sublytic C5b-9 and poly-C9 insertion that causes calcium influx, NFKB1 activation, and apoptotic RPE loss.
s2: The primary readout is retained apical surface CD59 with reduced C5b-9/C9 deposition by flow cytometry or immunofluorescence.

s1: Reduced PRMT1-mediated asymmetric dimethylation of the FUS RGG domains lowers the saturation threshold for FUS liquid-liquid phase separation, driving conversion of nuclear condensates into rigid gels that trap RNA polymerase II and splicing factors; enhancing PRMT1 activity or arginine methylation will disperse aberrant condensates and mitigate toxicity.
s2: Boosting mitophagy upstream of receptor phosphorylation is a rational bypass because ubiquitin amplification compensates for weakened TBK1-dependent OPTN activation.

s1: Oxidative glycation strips GPI-anchored CD59 from the RPE surface, removing the final checkpoint on terminal complement and permitting repeated sublytic C5b-9 and poly-C9 insertion that causes calcium influx, NFKB1 activation, and apoptotic RPE loss.
s2: Preserving CD59 should specifically prevent sublytic C5b-9 and poly-C9 insertion while leaving upstream complement surveillance intact.

s1: Oxidative and MMP9-mediated loss of membrane-bound CD59 from the aged RPE surface leaves C5b-9 assembly unopposed, producing sustained sublytic calcium influx that drives progressive RPE cell death.
s2: Readouts: surface CD59 retention by flow cytometry or surface biotinylation, soluble CD59 shedding in supernatants, C5b-9 neoepitope deposition by immunostaining, intracellular Ca2+ transients via Fluo-4 imaging, and RPE survival by TUNEL and LDH release.

s1: Loss of SIGMAR1 function disrupts ER-mitochondria contact sites, uncoupling ITPR1-VDAC1-HSPA9 calcium channeling and producing mitochondrial Ca2+ overload with PPIF-dependent permeability transition pore opening and cytochrome c release.
s2: Inhibit the peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase activity of PPIF (pharmacologically or by gene silencing) to raise the Ca2+ threshold for permeability transition pore opening, thereby decoupling MAM-driven Ca2+ dyshomeostasis from irreversible mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization.

s1: Mutant TIA1 and HNRNPA1, together with MATR3, slow G3BP1-nucleated stress granule disassembly and promote aberrant liquid-to-solid phase transitions that seed fibrillar aggregation of TDP-43 and FUS.
s2: Activate or potentiate the HSP70-family (HSPA8/HSPA1A)-HSPH1 disaggregase machinery with BAG3 co-chaperone support to accelerate disassembly of G3BP1-nucleated stress granules and dissolve maturing solid cores before they seed TDP-43/FUS fibrils.

s1: Extracellular phosphorylated TDP-43 seeds enter recipient neurons and glia via SDC2- and AGER-dependent uptake, templating seeded aggregation and propagating pathology trans-neuronally along connected circuits.
s2: SQSTM1/p62-mediated aggrephagy is a proven route for eliminating ubiquitinated RNP condensates and TDP-43 inclusions in motor neurons.

s1: Progressive depletion of nuclear TDP-43 (TARDBP) derepresses cryptic exon insertion into STMN2 and UNC13A pre-mRNAs, reducing functional stathmin-2 and MUNC13A protein and driving distal axon degeneration of motor neurons.
s2: Steric masking of the TDP-43-repressed cryptic splice acceptor and cryptic polyadenylation elements in STMN2 and UNC13A pre-mRNAs restores canonical splicing, reconstituting full-length stathmin-2 and MUNC13A protein and thereby protecting distal motor axons from degeneration.

s1: Age-related downregulation of the SLC7A11/SLC3A2 xCT cystine-glutamate antiporter limits cysteine supply for GCLC-dependent glutathione synthesis, leaving GPX4 unable to detoxify phospholipid hydroperoxides and triggering lipid-peroxidation-dependent ferroptotic RPE death in GA.
s2: Restoring iron export simultaneously relieves the GPX4-suppressive labile-iron burden and removes the substrate for ACSL4-driven lipid peroxide amplification, addressing the ferroptotic execution step implicated in GA enlargement rather than only its downstream inflammatory sequelae.

s1: Loss-of-function variants in complement regulators CFI and CFH together with gain-of-function C3/CFB alleles drive assembly of an intracellular C3 convertase (complosome) in RPE cells, causing autologous C3b deposition and sublytic C5b-9 (MAC) injury that kills RPE cells and enlarges geographic atrophy lesions.
s2: Inhibit C3/CFB convertase assembly inside RPE using a cell-penetrant compstatin-class C3 inhibitor (or intracellular CFB inhibitor) delivered to the RPE, optionally combined with restoration of CFI cofactor activity via RPE-targeted expression or recombinant factor I.

s1: C03 traces a coherent, literature-anchored causal chain from the most common genetic cause of ALS (C9orf72 DPRs) through NPM1 mislocalization and impaired ribosome biogenesis to nucleolar-stress-driven TP53 stabilization, giving etiologically specific mechanistic depth; C05 is grounded in real SIGMAR1/MAM and mPTP biology but is a more generic terminal blockade, conflates two etiologies (ultra-rare SIGMAR1 loss versus SOD1) whose Ca2+ phenotypes differ, and its claims of PPIF as 'obligate' and of SIGMAR1 loss causing matrix overload (rather than impaired Ca2+ transfer) are internally tense.
s2: C05 presents a more completely specified causal chain with a quantifiable effector node (PPIF-dependent Ca2+ threshold for mPTP opening) and a convergence argument that extends beyond the rare SIGMAR1 genotype to MAM/mitochondrial Ca2+ dyshomeostasis seen across ALS genotypes; C03 is anchored to the most common genetic cause, but its claim that NPM1 restoration is sufficient for rescue is less established, since arginine-rich DPRs exert toxicity through multiple parallel pathways, and it bundles two mechanistically distinct interventions.

s1: C03 is more concretely grounded in established histopathology and published biology—age/oxidative-stress-driven heparanase upregulation, HS chain loss in Bruch's membrane, and CFH's known GAG-binding domains (with the Y402H risk variant affecting HS binding)—forming a coherent causal chain to focal complement dysregulation at the atrophy site; C06 intracellular alternative-pathway convertase ('complosome') in RPE is plausible and genetically motivated but rests on weaker evidence that full convertase assembly and CFB are operative intracellularly in RPE.
s2: C06 builds the deeper genotype-to-phenotype causal chain, anchoring its intracellular convertase ('complosome') hypothesis in the strongest GA genetics (CFH/CFI loss-of-function, C3/CFB gain-of-function) and in the clinical validation of the C3 node by pegcetacoplan, whereas C03 CFH-heparan sulfate anchoring biochemistry is well grounded but its HPSE-driven etiology lacks direct genetic or clinical validation.

s1: C01 wins because it targets the defining and near-universal pathology of ALS—TDP-43 and hnRNPA1 RNP aggregation—with a precise molecular mechanism (m6A-triggered holdase chaperone activity of YTHDC1), positioning a single upstream factor above multiple disease-defining lesions; C06 cGAS-STING-neuroinflammation axis is mechanistically coherent but addresses a secondary/modifying pathology and the PINK1/PRKN-mtDNA-STING causal chain in ALS remains less directly established.
s2: C06 edges out because each link in its chain (mitophagy failure, cytosolic mtDNA, cGAS-STING activation, type I IFN/CXCL10 signatures) has direct documentation in ALS tissue and models, whereas C01 premise that nuclear YTHDC1 is reduced in ALS is hypothesized rather than established, though C01 anchoring to TDP-43/hnRNPA1 aggregation is compelling and both are mechanistically coherent; C06 main caveat is tension with TBK1 loss-of-function ALS genetics, which it partially sidesteps by inhibiting at STING.

s1: C06 offers a precise, genetically anchored causal chain (CFB/CFH and ARMS2/HTRA1 risk converging on CTSB-mediated intracellular C3 activation, mitochondrial C3b opsonization, and OXPHOS collapse) that directly explains why extracellular complement inhibitors only partially slow GA; C07 is disease-relevant but mechanistically looser, since SOAT1 is ER-resident and esterification is often protective against free-cholesterol toxicity, so the lysosomal-trapping logic is less coherent.
s2: C07 is anchored in well-established pathology (drusen unesterified/esterified cholesterol, lysosomal dysfunction in RPE aging) and validated AMD risk genetics (ABCA1, APOE, LIPC, CETP), with a coherent, previously demonstrated causal chain from SOAT1-driven esterification to lysosomal stalling; C06 cascade (CTSB cleavage of intracellular C3, mitochondrial C3b opsonization, OXPHOS collapse) draws on emerging complosome biology and plausibly explains the partial efficacy of extracellular complement inhibitors, but each link is individually less evidenced and the assembled chain is more speculative.

s1: C01 integrates the three best-established pillars of GA biology—Bruch's membrane HS loss with aging, the CFH Y402H risk variant's impaired GAG binding, and local alternative-pathway dysregulation—into one causal, testable chain, whereas C03 pyroptosis narrative is plausible but rests on a contested NLRP3/RPE death-mode literature.
s2: Both are mechanistically coherent; C03 rests on a well-documented RPE inflammasome-CASP1-GSDMD pyroptosis axis that is proximal to the cell loss defining GA, while C01 integrates Bruch's membrane heparan sulfate aging with CFH-dependent alternative-pathway dysregulation anchored to the strongest GA genetic risk factor, so neither clearly dominates despite C01 SULF1-redundancy and causality gaps versus C03 death-mode redundancy questions.

s1: C04 offers a coherent mitochondria-to-innate-immunity chain with strong ALS relevance (type I IFN signatures in CSF/spinal cord, mtDNA release from mitophagy failure, and genetic crosstalk via C9orf72 haploinsufficiency enhancing STING signaling), and it explicitly manages the TBK1 loss-of-function paradox by acting upstream at STING1. C08 draws on solid MAM genetics (SIGMAR1-E102Q, VAPB-ALS8) but its core Ca2+ logic is internally inconsistent: VAPB-PTPIP51 uncoupling is generally reported to reduce, not cause overload of, mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake, and the proposal simultaneously argues for restoring uptake and preventing overload.
s2: C08 earns the edge because its mechanism converges on two monogenic ALS genes (SIGMAR1 and VAPB) at a single structure (the VAPB-PTPIP51 MAM tether), giving an unusually direct genetic-to-structural rationale for cell-autonomous motor neuron death via Ca2+ dysregulation and mPTP; C04 cGAS-STING-IFN axis is coherent and well-argued, and its handling of the TBK1 loss-of-function paradox is sophisticated, but it rests on indirect convergence of mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammatory signatures rather than a direct causal genetic link.

s1: C03 offers a genotype-specific causal chain from the most common ALS mutation (C9orf72) through arginine-rich DPRs, NPM1 mislocalization, impaired ribosome biogenesis, and nucleolar stress-driven TP53 stabilization to motor neuron death, which is mechanistically deep and links toxic species to a defined upstream death trigger; C09 is plausible and rests on reported inflammasome activation in ALS tissue and SOD1 models, but it applies a generic neuroinflammatory module that is not ALS-specific and whose genetic-validation literature in SOD1G93A mice is more contested than stated.
s2: C09 is anchored in a causally validated node — NLRP3/CASP1 components are elevated in ALS tissue and genetic deletion of Nlrp3 or Casp1 attenuates SOD1G93A progression — and the aggregate-to-inflammasome-to-pyroptosis chain applies across SOD1, TDP-43, and sporadic disease, whereas C03 offers an articulate but more associative chain (DPR-NPM1-ribosome biogenesis-TP53) restricted to C9orf72 with the decisive NPM1 node not yet causally proven and the intervention confounded by combining NPM1 rescue with RAN-translation suppression.

s1: C10 offers the deeper mechanistic synthesis, converging ALS2 Rab5-GEF loss and CHMP2B ESCRT-III dysfunction onto a shared RAB7A-dependent node governing TrkB-BDNF retrograde trophic signaling, with TFEB as a defined druggable bypass; C09 haploinsufficiency model is coherent and genetics-anchored but essentially extends the familiar RNA-binding-protein paradigm.
s2: C10 provides a deeply specified causal chain (ALS2/Rab5 GEF loss + CHMP2B ESCRT-III dysfunction -> RAB7A-dependent maturation failure -> trapped TrkB-BDNF signaling endosomes -> somal CREB/ERK5 deprivation) that connects two real ALS genes to a defined neuronal death pathway, whereas C09 mechanism (ARPP21 loss collapses post-transcriptional programs) is plausible but shallower, hinges on a single recent genetic report, and leaves the loss-of-function versus toxic-gain-of-function ambiguity unresolved, which directly undercuts the gene-replacement logic.

s1: C07 grounds its mechanism in the strongest AMD genetic risk locus (CFH Y402H) and builds a coherent causal chain from failed alternative-pathway regulation to intracellular C3b opsonization, autophagic blockade, and C5AR1/C5b-9 sequelae, whereas C09 relies on well-documented iron/lipid-peroxidation findings in AMD tissue but lacks a genetic or disease-specific anchor and assembles a generic ferroptosis module.
s2: C09 assembles a fully supported causal chain (NCOA4/TFRC labile iron, ACSL4-driven PUFA-PE substrate, SLC7A11-GSH-GPX4 decline) that maps onto documented iron deposition, ferritin induction, and lipid-peroxidation products in GA RPE, whereas C07 is anchored in the strongest genetic risk factor (CFH Y402H) and clinically validated complement biology but its central premise, a pathogenic endolysosomal C3bBb convertase that diverts autophagy, rests on extrapolation with limited direct evidence.

s1: C01 holds a slight edge because every link of its mTORC1→TFEB/TFE3→CLEAR-network→autophagic-flux cascade is independently validated and maps directly onto hallmark RPE pathology (lipofuscin, undegraded outer segments, mitochondrial debris), whereas C06 chain, despite a strong human anchor in aceruloplasminemia maculopathy and donor-tissue peroxidation data, leans on a less firmly established age-related HAMP/CP-insufficiency premise and on ferroptosis causality in GA that remains largely correlative.
s2: C06 presents a tightly coupled, multi-level causal chain—ferroxidase/hepcidin insufficiency, labile Fe2+, DHA-rich outer-segment peroxidation to 4-HNE/F2-isoprostanes, GPX4 inactivation, ACSL4-dependent ferroptosis—that is anchored by human genetic evidence (aceruloplasminemia maculopathy) and donor-tissue chemistry in GA; C01 TFEB/lysosome axis is credible and disease-relevant but rests on a more generic aging narrative (mTORC1 hyperactivity driving TFEB retention in GA) with less donor-level validation and no explanation of the origin of accumulated damage.

s1: C05 traces an internally consistent, literature-supported causal chain from a bona fide ALS gene (SIGMAR1) through MAM Ca2+ dyshomeostasis to a defined terminal executor (CypD-gated mPTP and cytochrome c release), with explicit cross-subtype logic (SOD1 mitochondria) and a coherent cell-vulnerability argument, whereas C10 NEK1-DNA repair rationale is plausible but rests on a still-debated disease-relevant function (repair vs. ciliary roles), contested penetrance of NEK1 haploinsufficiency, and an ATM-TP53 degeneration cascade not yet demonstrated in vivo.
s2: C10 wins for stronger disease-relevant genetic causality—NEK1 is among the most prevalent monogenic ALS causes, and the pathway from haploinsufficiency through DNA repair failure to ATM-TP53 apoptosis is a coherent, testable causal chain addressing the primary lesion; C05 mitochondrial biology is well-characterized but represents a more generic cytoprotective strategy tied to a rare SIGMAR1 subtype, with generalization to SOD1 ALS diluting mechanistic specificity.

s1: C01 is anchored in the best-supported disease architecture — CFH loss-of-function/CFB gain-of-function driving unrestrained extracellular alternative-pathway amplification — and its causal logic is directly validated by the Cfh-/-;Cfb+/- rescue of retinal C3 deposition, placing one intervention upstream of opsonization, MAC, and C5a chemotaxis; C06 intracellular 'complosome' convertase hypothesis is conceptually rich and could explain the partial efficacy of extracellular inhibitors, but intracellular C3/CFB convertase assembly and sublytic C5b-9 formation within RPE remain poorly evidenced and partly speculative.
s2: C06 goes deeper mechanistically by integrating the complosome concept—intracellular alternative-pathway convertase assembly in RPE—with the CFH/CFI-LOF and C3/CFB-GOF genetic architecture and the partial efficacy of extracellular pegcetacoplan, explicitly explaining an unaddressed disease compartment; C01 is a coherent but conventional extracellular amplification-blockade model.

s1: C08 offers a coherent, histopathologically grounded chain from drusen cholesteryl-ester accumulation through age-declining LXR/ABCA1/APOE efflux to impaired phagocytosis, while C10 anchors iron-driven RPE injury in strong human and mouse genetic validation (aceruloplasminemia, Cp-null retinal degeneration) plus a defined death pathway (GPX4/SLC7A11 ferroptosis); both premises carry caveats (APOE4 is paradoxically protective in AMD; persistence of TFRC import in iron-loaded aged RPE is asserted more than documented), so this is a tie.
s2: C10 rests on a single, genetically and histopathologically validated node — aceruloplasminemia directly proves CP-loss-driven retinal iron overload suffices for RPE degeneration, and iron as the substrate for Fenton-driven lipid peroxidation gives a direct, quantifiable causal chain to ferroptotic RPE death; C08 cholesterol-efflux narrative is plausible and drusen-supported, but the causal link from LXR/ABCA1/APOE attenuation to RPE death is more diffuse, involves a multi-target axis, and is complicated by APOE isoform biology (APOE4 being protective in AMD).

s1: C04 is grounded in a well-validated mechanistic cascade—oxidized mtDNA release activating cGAS-STING-IRF3 signaling in RPE, with published preclinical evidence that genetic or pharmacologic ablation of this axis reduces retinal degeneration and links CXCL10 to human AMD ocular fluids; C06 intracellular complement/CTSB-C3b-mitochondrial axis is conceptually rich and integrates genetic risk alleles elegantly, but the specific causal chain (CTSB as the dominant intracellular C3 convertase-equivalent node, mitochondrial C3b as the proximal mediator of OXPHOS collapse driving GA) remains more preliminary and less supported by loss-of-function rescue data in retinal degeneration models.
s2: C06 offers a deeper, more causally specific chain—CTSB-mediated intracellular C3 cleavage to C3b, mitochondrial opsonization, and OXPHOS collapse—grounded in the emerging complosome literature and explicitly explaining why extracellular complement inhibitors (pegcetacoplan) only partially slow GA, while integrating both CFH and ARMS2/HTRA1 risk axes onto a single proximal enzymatic node. C04 mtDNA-cGAS-STING-senescence cascade is coherent and supported by preclinical data but is a more generic inflammatory axis transplanted from broader senescence/interferon biology.

s1: C04 offers a deeper, cell-autonomous mechanism that causally links a defined ALS genotype (VCP segregase failure) to stress-granule persistence and TDP-43/FUS aggregation, with a coherent bypass rationale via TFEB-driven aggrephagy; C09 is a well-validated but comparatively generic neuroinflammatory cascade whose individual steps (NLRP3-NEK7-CASP1-GSDMD) are largely imported from broader inflammasome biology.
s2: C09 rests on a fully specified, causally validated cascade with human postmortem data and in vivo genetic loss-of-function evidence (Nlrp3/Casp1 deletion attenuating SOD1G93A disease), whereas C04 elegant VCP-refractory condensate model is mechanistically deep but rests on a contested stress-granule persistence premise with no cited causal evidence that TFEB activation rescues disease.

s1: C01 offers a coherent, multi-node causal chain (HAMP→SLC40A1 internalization→labile iron→GPX4 inactivation→ACSL4-driven ferroptosis) anchored in documented RPE/Bruch's iron accumulation and Cp/Heph mutant degeneration rescued by chelation, with an explicit cell-death execution step tied to GA enlargement; C07 rests on solid GWAS/drusen lipid evidence but its mechanism is partially self-undermining (relies on 'residual' ABCA1/ABCG1 efflux despite positing their decline, and SOAT1 blockade raises free cholesterol that is itself lysosomotoxic) and defines no executional path to atrophy.
s2: C07 presents a tighter, more directly evidenced causal chain: cholesterol/cholesteryl-ester entrapment in RPE lysosomes is documented in drusen and GA, HDL-trafficking loci (APOE, LIPC, CETP) are validated AMD risk genes, and SOAT1 inhibition has already reduced sub-RPE lipid deposits in AMD-like models, whereas C01 ferroptosis-execution link to GA lesion enlargement rests on more inferential connections (ocular hepcidin excess driving SLC40A1 internalization specifically in human GA).

s1: C01 rests on a deeply documented chain — aging-linked mTORC1 activation retaining TFEB/TFE3 in the cytoplasm, suppressed CLEAR-network transcription, and lysosomal/autophagic failure causing outer-segment and mitochondrial debris accumulation in RPE — that maps directly onto the lipofuscin/drusen pathology defining GA; C05 CNN2→actomyosin→MERTK phagocytosis axis is coherent and integrates adhesion and barrier failure, but the causal chain is longer, each link less independently validated, and disease relevance hinges on newer, less mature genetic evidence.
s2: Both mechanisms are coherent and disease-relevant — C05 offers a genetically anchored, loss-of-function causal chain (CNN2 haploinsufficiency → actomyosin/MERTK phagocytosis failure → lipofuscin-driven RPE decompensation) with high specificity to RPE cell biology, while C01 rests on the deeply validated mTORC1–TFEB/lysosomal-biogenesis axis that integrates lipofuscin, POS clearance, and mitophagy; neither dominates, so tie.

s1: C05 is anchored in the strongest human genetic risk locus for GA (CFH Y402H), with a coherent causal chain to the observed C3b/C5b-9 deposition on RPE/choriocapillaris, whereas C07 MTORC1-hyperactivity-as-bottleneck premise is plausible but less directly validated in human GA, and TFEB-driven biogenesis may not clear largely indigestible bisretinoids (and could even promote basolateral exocytosis to Bruch's membrane).
s2: C05 is anchored in the strongest human genetic association for GA (CFH Y402H at rs1061170) and the actual histopathologic signature (C3b/iC3b and C5b-9 on RPE/choriocapillaris), with each mechanistic step (convertase decay, CFI cofactor activity, heparan-sulfate surface binding) experimentally established, whereas C07 premise that MTORC1-driven TFEB sequestration is the causal bottleneck in aged RPE is asserted rather than demonstrated, though its lysosomal-intoxication model is biologically coherent.

s1: C06 builds on well-grounded m6A-YTHDF phase-separation biology and the established ATXN2-polyQ/stress-granule ALS link, and its intervention (removing m6A-reader reinforcement) cleanly matches the hypothesized maturation step; C07 R-loop/DNA-repair cascade has strong causal anchors (SETX, FUS repair defects, RNASEH1 rescue) but its plan to pharmacologically enhance PARP1 catalytic activity conflicts with evidence that PARP hyperactivation is itself neurotoxic in ALS models, weakening internal coherence.
s2: C07 wins because it rests on a direct causal chain anchored by genetics—SETX is a bona fide ALS4 gene, FUS/TDP-43 nuclear depletion impairing PARP1-XRCC1 repair is experimentally supported, and the R-loop-to-DSB-to-TP53 apoptosis pathway has been demonstrated in ALS models—whereas C06 requirement that m6A marks drive granule maturation in ATXN2-polyQ motor neurons is plausible but more inferential, and the ATXN2 link to METTL3 is indirect.

s1: C04 offers a multi-tiered causal chain anchored in direct prior evidence (Alu-RNA/cGAS-driven RPE degeneration, STING-IRF3-IFNB1-CXCL10 signaling) and explains the pathognomonic expanding cytotoxic border via CXCR3+ CD8/NK recruitment, whereas C05 assembles a coherent but more generically transplanted ferroptosis axis supported mainly by correlative human data (iron, 4-HNE, GPX4) without equally direct human GA pathway evidence.
s2: C05 integrates a cell-autonomous death axis (NCOA4 ferritinophagy, GPX4 loss, ACSL4-dependent PUFA-phospholipid loading) in which every arrow is established ferroptosis biochemistry, anchors it to documented GA findings (retinal iron accumulation, 4-HNE/MDA adducts), and targets a rate-limiting druggable enzyme with quantitative lipidomic PD readouts; C04 is anchored to genuinely compelling human histology (cGAS-STING activation and CD8/NK cells at the atrophic margin) but stacks several unproven causal arrows (STING-IFNB1 as dominant output, CXCL10 as dominant chemokine, CXCR3-dependent recruitment as the lesion driver) and underplays IRF3-independent STING outputs such as inflammasome activation that dominate the RPE AMD literature, so C05 wins narrowly.

s1: C03 presents a tight, linear causal chain (drusen/bisretinoid lysosomal rupture to NLRP3-CASP1-GSDMD) anchored at the atrophy margin, and its executor-level blockade preserves upstream homeostatic outputs like IL18, a mechanistically elegant distinction; C06 multi-node ferroptosis argument is coherent but rests on a partially circular oxidative-stress premise (oxidative load both suppresses SLC7A11 and inactivates GPX4) and is less resolved mechanistically.
s2: C06 is deeper and better anchored in RPE-specific physiology, tying constitutive phagocytosis of PUFA-rich outer segments, documented retinal iron accumulation, and GPX4/SLC7A11 essentiality into a coherent initiating-plus-executing death pathway, whereas C03 inflammasome-centric narrative, while coherent and cell-type-restricted, rests on a more contested literature in which NLRP3 roles in AMD models have proven double-edged.

s1: C02 goes beyond restating complement dysregulation by proposing a specific self-propagating EV-mtDNA/TLR9-STING loop that plausibly explains both the centrifugal enlargement pattern of GA and the residual ~65-80% progression on C3/C5 inhibitors, integrating complement injury with innate nucleic-acid sensing; C05 is mechanistically sound but largely reiterates the canonical alternative-pathway overactivation narrative.
s2: C02 integrates complement injury, oxidized mtDNA-bearing CD63+ EVs, and TLR9/STING sensing into a self-propagating circuit that plausibly explains both centrifugal GA enlargement and the only ~20-35% slowing achieved by approved C3/C5 inhibitors, whereas C05 restates the canonical alternative-pathway dysregulation narrative and is technically imprecise (an SCR1-4 fragment lacks the SCR7/19-20 surface-targeting domains whose Y402H impairment is the core defect).

s1: C01 wins by integrating the strongest GA evidence base (alternative complement activation, CFH haploinsufficiency/Y402H as top genetic risk) with a concrete extracellular aging mechanism (SULF2-mediated 6-O-desulfation of perlecan HS erasing CFH docking sites), explaining how aging can phenocopy genetic CFH dysfunction locally; C04 is coherent and grounded (DICER1 loss, Alu accumulation) but leans on a less clinically validated type I IFN axis and must compete with the originally implicated NLRP3/MyD88 pathway downstream of Alu RNA.
s2: C04 rests on a well-documented causal chain (DICER1 loss, cytosolic Alu RNA/DNA, cGAS-STING-driven interferon signaling and RPE degeneration) with published in vivo sufficiency data, whereas C01 perlecan desulfation-SULF2-CFH link is coherent and grounded in known CFH-heparan sulfate biology but the specific causal role of SULF2 in Bruch's membrane aging and GA remains largely hypothetical.

s1: C06 grounds its mechanism in a single genetically validated lesion (SPG11 biallelic loss) with a short causal chain from spatacsin deficiency to autophagosome maturation failure, and TFEB activation is the canonical bypass for that proximal defect; C10 chain from ALS2/CHMP2B through RAB7A to TrkB-BDNF retrograde trophic deprivation is biologically plausible but conflates two distinct genetic subtypes and rests on more speculative links (e.g., TFEB-driven RAB7A upregulation rescuing signaling endosome delivery).
s2: C10 provides a deeper, multi-layered causal chain linking two genetically validated ALS lesions (ALS2 Rab5-GEF loss, CHMP2B ESCRT-III dysfunction) through RAB7A-dependent endosome maturation to a specific, measurable neuronal output—retrograde TrkB-BDNF signaling endosome delivery and somatic CREB/ERK5 activation—which is well grounded in established TrkB trafficking and BDNF retrograde signaling literature. C06 mechanism (SPG11 loss impairs autophagosome maturation; TFEB boosts lysosomal capacity to clear aggregates) is coherent but comparatively generic, and the cited PMIDs appear dubious/unsupported, weakening its evidentiary grounding.

s1: C04 is anchored in published causal data (MMP9 upregulation in fast-fatigable motor neurons pre-onset, with Mmp9 loss delaying denervation and extending survival in SOD1 mice) and extends it via a biochemically plausible, substrate-specific mechanism (gelatinase cleavage of collagen IV/laminin at the NMJ basement membrane), matching the known distal-first pathophysiology of ALS. C10 chain (NEK1 haploinsufficiency -> ATR-CHEK1 impairment -> DSB accumulation -> TP53 apoptosis) rests on weaker causal evidence: heterozygous NEK1 loss is mostly a risk factor ( modest odds ratio), not an established monogenic cause as claimed, and DDR failure as the driver of motor neuron death in NEK1-ALS is unproven, benefiting only a small patient subset.
s2: C10 is anchored in robust human genetics (NEK1 haploinsufficiency as a bona fide ALS cause) with a well-defined signaling cascade (ATR-CHEK1, homologous recombination, TP53 apoptosis) supported by published NEK1 biology, whereas C04 core premise (MMP9 upregulation in fast-fatigable motor neurons) is solid but its specific LAMB2/COL4A2-proteolysis mechanism at the NMJ is speculative and largely SOD1-model-centric.

s1: Age-related SULF2-mediated desulfation of heparan sulfate chains on HSPG2 in Bruch's membrane reduces CFH docking sites, diminishing local alternative-pathway complement regulation and permitting C3 activation and C5b-9 deposition on RPE and choriocapillaris.
s2: Geographic atrophy is characterized by unchecked alternative-pathway activation with C3 activation products and C5b-9 deposition on RPE and choriocapillaris, and CFH haploinsufficiency is a major genetic risk factor.

s1: Misfolded mutant SOD1 associates with the mitochondrial outer membrane at VDAC1 and BCL2, depressing electron transport chain complex I activity and ATP production while increasing superoxide generation in motor neurons.
s2: MMP9 is selectively upregulated in vulnerable fast-fatigable motor neurons early in ALS, prior to symptom onset, and its loss delays muscle denervation and extends survival in SOD1 models.

s1: Extracellular phosphorylated TDP-43 seeds enter recipient neurons and glia via SDC2- and AGER-dependent uptake, templating seeded aggregation and propagating pathology trans-neuronally along connected circuits.
s2: Misfolded SOD1 and TDP-43 aggregates act as danger signals that drive NLRP3-NEK7-dependent inflammasome assembly in spinal microglia, activating CASP1 to mature IL1B/IL18 and cleave GSDMD, causing pyroptotic release of inflammatory mediators that accelerates motor neuron degeneration.

s1: Defective CCS-mediated copper loading and ATP7A-dependent copper trafficking leave SOD1 in the apo, aggregation-prone state, promoting misfolding that CuATSM copper delivery or SOD1 dimer-stabilizing aggregation inhibitors can rescue.
s2: In vitro, use ALS patient iPSC-derived microglia co-cultured with iPSC motor neurons, challenge with mtDNA or SOD1 aggregates, and quantify ISG induction and motor neuron survival rescue by STING or CGAS inhibition.

s1: Mutant VCP p97 segregase fails to extract ubiquitinated components from G3BP1-positive stress granules and ERAD substrates, prolonging ribonucleoprotein condensate lifetime and converting liquid-like granules into seeds for irreversible TDP-43 and FUS aggregation with UBQLN2 cofactor dysfunction.
s2: Use iPSC-derived motor neurons from ALS patients carrying VCP R155H or A232E mutations, induce stress granules with sodium arsenite, then monitor disassembly kinetics after stress washout via live-cell imaging of G3BP1-GFP.

s1: Extracellular phosphorylated TDP-43 aggregates are taken up by recipient neurons and glia via LRP1-mediated endocytosis, seeding templated misfolding that propagates pathology along neuroanatomic circuits in a prion-like manner.
s2: Primary readouts: FRAP recovery of G3BP1-GFP granules as a liquid-versus-solid metric, filter-trap and detergent-insoluble fraction quantification of TDP-43, m6A profiling (MeRIP-seq/miCLIP) of stress-granule transcripts, and neuronal survival and neurite integrity as functional endpoints.

s1: PFN1 loss-of-function reduces actin monomer sequestration while TUBA4A mutations destabilize the tubulin heterodimer pool, collapsing cytoskeletal dynamics, impairing growth-cone turnover, and promoting sequestration of TDP-43 into insoluble inclusions.
s2: This approach is agnostic to the cause of TDP-43 loss and acts at a single well-validated genomic locus rather than attempting global TDP-43 relocalization.

s1: Extracellular phosphorylated TDP-43 aggregates are taken up by recipient neurons and glia via LRP1-mediated endocytosis, seeding templated misfolding that propagates pathology along neuroanatomic circuits in a prion-like manner.
s2: Use isogenic human iPSC-derived motor neurons carrying FUS R521C or TDP-43 mislocalizing variants, or chemically induced mislocalization, with RNASEH1 delivered via inducible overexpression or AAV.

s1: Loss of the arginine-glycine-rich RNA-binding protein ARPP21 disrupts post-transcriptional regulation and localization of its target mRNAs in motor neurons, impairing neuronal translational programs and lowering the threshold for neurodegeneration.
s2: ARPP21 loss would phenocopy the convergent ALS biology of defective RNA metabolism seen with TDP-43, FUS and hnRNPA1, lowering the threshold for motor neuron degeneration.

s1: Loss-of-function ARPP21 variants newly linked to familial ALS reduce RNA-binding stabilization of motor-neuron transcripts including components of the TDP-43/hnRNP regulatory network, leading to RNA dysregulation that increases aggregation-prone ribonucleoprotein assembly and neurodegeneration.
s2: Boosting a single endogenous chaperone could simultaneously suppress HNRNPA1 and TDP-43 aggregation rather than targeting each client protein separately.

s1: Extracellular phosphorylated TDP-43 seeds enter recipient neurons and glia via SDC2- and AGER-dependent uptake, templating seeded aggregation and propagating pathology trans-neuronally along connected circuits.
s2: Antagonize or downregulate SDC2 and AGER receptor activity to prevent uptake of extracellular phosphorylated TDP-43 seeds, thereby interrupting the cell-to-cell propagation cycle while allowing native TARDBP function to continue.

s1: C9orf72 dipeptide repeats and TDP-43 pathology disrupt RANGAP1/KPNB1-dependent nuclear import and degrade nucleoporins (POM121, NUP62), causing cytoplasmic TDP-43 mislocalization that simultaneously worsens toxic gain-of-function and nuclear depletion.
s2: C9orf72 repeat expansions are the most common genetic cause of ALS, and poly(GR) dipeptide repeats are a well-documented, dose-toxic gain-of-function product whose nucleolar localization is a conserved pathology hallmark.

s1: Cytoplasmic mislocalization of TDP-43 (TARDBP) abolishes its nuclear splicing-repressor function, permitting cryptic exon inclusion that suppresses STMN2 and UNC13A transcripts and thereby impairs axon repair and neurotransmitter release in motor neurons.
s2: If SDC2 and AGER serve as the principal entry portals for extracellular TDP-43 seeds, their functional blockade would decouple seeded aggregation from trans-neuronal transmission, slowing disease propagation.

s1: Age-related upregulation of heparanase (HPSE) strips sulfated heparan sulfate chains from HSPG2 (perlecan)/syndecan proteoglycans in Bruch's membrane, reducing CFH anchoring and amplifying alternative-pathway complement injury to RPE and choriocapillaris in GA.
s2: In vivo, use aged C57BL/6J or Ccl2-/-/Cx3cr1-/- GA-model mice with intravitreal HPSE inhibitor versus vehicle, reading out HPSE activity and HS stubs in Bruch's membrane, CFH/MAC immunolocalization by confocal microscopy, quantitative OCT and fundus autofluorescence for atrophy area, and ERG for retinal function, with endpoint comparison at 3 and 6 months.

s1: Dissociation of the VAPB-RMDN3 endoplasmic reticulum-mitochondria tether reduces ITPR3-VDAC1-mediated Ca2+ and phospholipid transfer, depressing oxidative phosphorylation in motor neurons.
s2: Restoring SIGMAR1 activity therefore addresses a proximal, genetically validated node upstream of the Ca2+ and bioenergetic failure described in the hypothesis.

s1: Loss-of-function CFH variation combined with CFB gain-of-function causes unrestrained alternative-pathway complement activation on RPE and Bruch's membrane, generating C3b/iC3b opsonization and C5b-9 (MAC)-mediated RPE lysis while C5a-C5AR1 signaling recruits CCR2+ inflammatory monocytes that together accelerate GA lesion expansion.
s2: Engineer human iPSC-derived RPE carrying AMD risk haplotypes (e.g., CFH Y402H, CFI R402H, C3 R102G) or CRISPR CFI knockdown, expose to oxidative/AMD-like stress, and read out intracellular C3b/iC3b and C5b-9 by confocal microscopy and flow cytometry, with RPE survival (caspase-3, LDH) and transepithelial resistance as functional endpoints; demonstrate dose-dependent rescue by cell-penetrant compstatin (Cp40 analog) or CFB siRNA.

s1: Chronic protein-folding stress in the RPE endoplasmic reticulum overactivates the EIF2AK3(PERK)-EIF2A-ATF4-DDIT3(CHOP) apoptotic arm of the unfolded protein response while XBP1/HSPA5-mediated adaptive resolution fails, driving CHOP-dependent RPE apoptosis.
s2: Locally (intravitreal or topical) inhibit STING1 with a small-molecule antagonist (palmitoylation-site inhibitor class, e.g., H-151 analogs), with MB21D1 enzymatic inhibitors as a backup arm, to extinguish the downstream type I IFN–CXCL10 gradient without systemic immunosuppression.

s1: Cytosolic oxidized mitochondrial DNA leaking from damaged RPE mitochondria activates the MB21D1(cGAS)-STING1-TBK1-IRF3 axis, inducing IFNB1 and CXCL10 interferon-stimulated responses that promote RPE dysfunction, senescence, and microglia-supported atrophic lesion growth.
s2: Inhibit the enzymatic activity of MB21D1 (cGAS) with a small-molecule antagonist delivered intravitreally or subretinally to attenuate STING1-dependent type I interferon signaling in RPE cells.

s1: Stressed RPE sheds exosomes enriched in complement C3 and miR-155 with reduced miR-146a, whose uptake by choroidal macrophages and endothelium represses SOCS1 and unleashes IRAK1/NFKB signaling, boosting macrophage TNF/IL6 output that feeds back onto RPE.
s2: Factor B is the obligate catalytic subunit of the alternative-pathway C3 and C5 convertases, so CFB inhibition acts upstream of every effector arm in the hypothesis (opsonization, MAC lysis, C5a-C5AR1 chemotaxis) with a single intervention.

s1: Haploinsufficiency of NEK1, augmented by C21ORF2 variants, weakens DNA single-strand break and base-excision repair in projection neurons, causing γH2AX-marked damage accumulation that triggers ATM-TP53-dependent degeneration.
s2: Restoring NEK1 dosage and kinase activity in ALS-vulnerable projection neurons re-enables efficient single-strand break and base-excision repair, preventing the γH2AX-marked damage accumulation that activates ATM-TP53-dependent degeneration.

s1: Loss of nuclear TDP-43 (TARDBP) function drives cryptic exon inclusion in STMN2 and UNC13A pre-mRNAs, depleting functional stathmin-2 and UNC13A protein and thereby impairing axonal regeneration and synaptic vesicle release in motor neurons.
s2: Primary readouts: automated immunofluorescence quantification of TDP-43 nuclear/cytoplasmic ratio, an NES-NLS-GFP nuclear import shuttle reporter, and western blot levels of POM121/NUP62; secondary readouts of nuclear RanGAP1 localization and motor neuron survival under chronic DPR exposure.

s1: Extracellular phosphorylated TDP-43 aggregates are taken up by recipient neurons and glia via LRP1-mediated endocytosis, seeding templated misfolding that propagates pathology along neuroanatomic circuits in a prion-like manner.
s2: In vivo progression is possible in TDP-43-dependent mouse models (e.g., TDP-43(Q331K) or rNLS8 lines) with endpoint readouts of cryptic exon inclusion in spinal cord and motor unit integrity by electromyography and survival.

s1: AMD-associated TREM2 risk alleles blunt TREM2-TYROBP signaling in subretinal myeloid cells, shifting them toward an SPP1(osteopontin)-high pro-inflammatory phenotype whose SPP1-CD44/ITGAV signaling on RPE elevates CXCL10 and MMP9 output and accelerates GA-margin tissue destruction.
s2: Locally (intravitreal or topical) inhibit STING1 with a small-molecule antagonist (palmitoylation-site inhibitor class, e.g., H-151 analogs), with MB21D1 enzymatic inhibitors as a backup arm, to extinguish the downstream type I IFN–CXCL10 gradient without systemic immunosuppression.

s1: RAN-translated poly(GA) dipeptide-repeat proteins from the C9orf72 expansion directly inhibit PSMB5 proteasome catalytic activity and overwhelm aggregate-clearance capacity, producing gain-of-function proteotoxic stress that kills motor neurons.
s2: Test in SOD1-G93A mice (and an independent mutant, e.g., TDP-43 or C9orf72 models) treated pre-symptomatically with an MMP-9-selective inhibitor or AAV-TIMP1.

s1: Oxidative nitration-mediated loss of membrane-bound CD59 on RPE cells permits persistent sublytic C5b-9 insertion, driving Ca2+ influx, arachidonic-acid release, and an IL6/CXCL8 secretory state that culminates in RPE apoptosis and choriocapillaris injury.
s2: Activate or restore functional CD59 expression on the RPE plasma membrane via gene delivery or membrane-anchored recombinant CD59 replacement, re-establishing host inhibition of terminal complement assembly at the RPE-choroid interface.

s1: C01 is anchored in the near-universal TDP-43 pathology of ALS, with human spinal-tissue and single-nucleus evidence that STMN2 cryptic splicing tracks disease, and its bypass logic (restoring a critical axon-maintenance factor downstream of TDP-43 loss) is mechanistically direct; C06 rests on a real but contested literature (GluR2 Q/R editing deficits reported in sALS but not always replicated) and invokes a classic, clinically translation-resistant excitotoxicity cascade, so C01 edges out on disease relevance despite C06 strong Adar2-conditional-knockout causal data.
s2: C06 offers a deeply elaborated causal cascade (ADARB1 loss -> unedited GRIA2 -> Ca2+-permeable AMPARs -> calpain/caspase death) with strong genetic validation, but its 'root cause' framing is weakened because ADARB1 downregulation is itself often downstream of TDP-43 dysfunction and the editing deficit is seen in a subset of cases; C01 is anchored to the defining TDP-43 pathology present in ~97% of ALS and specifies a precise molecular lesion (cryptic splice acceptor/polyA cassette), though it is a one-target bypass of a multifocal splicing collapse, so the criteria balance to a tie.

s1: C06 rests on the most directly validated axis in GA biology—complement risk genetics, MAC deposition in RPE/choroid, and documented oxidative CD59 loss—yielding a tight causal chain (CD59 loss → sublytic C5b-9 → Ca2+/arachidonate → IL6/CXCL8 → apoptosis), whereas C04 relevance is inferred from interferon signatures in models and only indirectly from TMEM173 gain-of-function vasculopathy rather than GA-specific human genetics.
s2: C06 presents a tighter, human-validated causal chain—CD59 nitration/loss is a documented early lesion in AMD donor tissue, sublytic C5b-9 effects on RPE (Ca2+ influx, IL-6/IL-8, apoptosis) are well characterized, and it addresses the known failure mode of global complement blockade by correcting a specific local deficit; C04 cGAS-STING axis in GA is plausible but rests on more correlative evidence (interferon signatures, microgliosis), and its claim that TMEM173 gain-of-function demonstrates tolerability of blockade is logically loose, since SAVI shows the consequence of activation, not inhibition.

s1: C02 is anchored in the near-universal TDP-43 nuclear-depletion pathology with causal, genetically supported downstream effectors (STMN2 axonal repair loss; UNC13A, a GWAS progression-risk locus, synaptic vesicle priming), giving a direct molecular chain from core disease mechanism to neuronal dysfunction; C09 Treg/microglial axis is well supported but rests on correlative immune biomarkers and modulates progression tempo rather than a core pathogenic driver.
s2: C02 addresses the core, near-universal pathology of ALS (TDP-43 nuclear depletion) with direct genetic validation (STMN2 loss abolishing axonal regeneration, UNC13A risk variants accelerating progression), providing a causal chain from proteinopathy to splice errors to neuronal dysfunction; C09 Treg-microglia axis is well described but remains a correlative, peripheral immunomodulatory mechanism.

s1: C06 integrates a validated ALS genetic risk factor (ATXN2 polyQ) with the core TDP-43/hnRNPA1 aggregation pathology via a specific, mechanistically rich condensate-maturation loop (METTL3-m6A-YTHDF2/3 low-complexity-domain reinforcement), whereas C10 assembles a plausible but more derivative chain from well-known injury-signaling (JNK-cargo release) and long-established axonal-transport-deficit models whose causal link to ALS progression is less novel mechanistically.
s2: C10 rests on a well-documented causal chain—JNK/MAPK10 phosphorylation of kinesin light chains/JIP adaptors releasing cargo, ALS-linked KIF5A tail mutations, DCTN1/DYNC1H1 retrograde deficits, and NEFH accumulation—all converging on the early distal axonopathy that genuinely precedes motor neuron loss; C06 m6A-YTHDF-SG axis is plausible and ATXN2-linked, but the critical liquid-to-solid 'maturation reinforcement' step is speculative and its claim of sparing acute protective granule assembly sits uneasily with reports that m6A/METTL3 promotes granule formation.

s1: C03 wins because it articulates a specific, multi-step molecular cascade (TDP-43/FUS-driven GSK3B activation, VAPB phosphorylation, VAPB-RMDN3 tether dissolution, ITPR3-VDAC1 Ca2+/lipid transfer failure, bioenergetic collapse) that is experimentally grounded and converges familial (VAPB/ALS8) and sporadic (TDP-43-positive ~97% of cases) ALS onto one mechanism; C10 is coherent but relies on NEK1's DNA-repair function being the disease-relevant one, which remains less established given NEK1's pleiotropy and the low penetrance of NEK1 variants.
s2: C03 edges out C10 because its mechanism (TDP-43/FUS-driven GSK3B activation dissolving the VAPB-RMDN3 tether, impairing ITPR3-VDAC1 Ca2+/lipid transfer and OXPHOS) is a multilayer, experimentally documented path converging on pathology present in ~97% of ALS cases, whereas C10 DNA-repair cascade is cleanly logical but rests on a narrower genetic lesion (~2-3% of cases) and on the still-debated premise that defective HR repair, rather than NEK1's other functions, drives motor neuron loss (Nek1+/- mice lack a robust spontaneous ALS phenotype).

s1: C07 provides a more integrated causal chain linking the primary ALS pathology (FUS/TDP-43 nuclear depletion) directly to R-loop accumulation, PARP1-XRCC1 repair failure, and p53-dependent neuronal death, with strong genetic validation through SETX-linked ALS. C10 assembles a plausible but more speculative compilation of transport pathway interactions, and its core therapeutic logic—preserving anterograde flux despite retrograde collapse—does not address whether cargo retention alone can compensate.
s2: C07 chain from FUS/TDP-43 mislocalization to R-loop accumulation, PARP1-XRCC1 repair failure, and TP53-dependent death is linear, anchored in core ALS pathology, and genetically validated by SETX-linked ALS plus published rescue of FUS-mutant toxicity by RNaseH1, whereas C10 compiles plausible transport components but its central claim that preserving anterograde coupling 'rebalances' flux despite retrograde impairment is internally less coherent.

s1: C07 offers a deeper, multi-tier causal chain (MTORC1-driven TFEB sequestration to CLEAR-network biogenesis, ATG7 flux, and PNPLA2/LAMP2 lipophagy) aimed at the hallmark lysosomal-lipofuscin substrate of GA, whereas C09 is a narrower terminal-execution pathway that hinges on an unquantified necroptotic contribution and CASP8 failure in vivo, though its pMLKL lesion-edge evidence is a strong human anchor.
s2: Both are mechanistically deep and disease-relevant; C09 offers a crisp execution-pathway logic (CASP8 checkpoint loss to RIPK1-RIPK3-MLKL rupture) directly coupled to centrifugal lesion enlargement and cites human pMLKL at GA borders, while C07 grounds itself in the classic lysosomal-insufficiency/lipofuscin pathology and a master regulatory axis; each has one speculative link (functional RIPK3 in RPE for C09, whether TFEB restoration suffices in advanced disease for C07), so this is a tie.

s1: Both mechanisms are well-grounded and mechanistically coherent. C05 identifies a precisely defined upstream convergence point (RAN gradient) with strong causal evidence in C9orf72 models, but its relevance is largely restricted to repeat-expansion ALS. C10 integrates KIF5A genetics, JNK-KLC biochemistry, retrograde impairment, and NEFH accumulation into a unifying dying-back axonopathy framework applicable across multiple ALS subtypes. The balance of depth versus breadth makes this a tie.
s2: C10 integrates human genetics (tail-domain KIF5A ALS mutations), stress-activated JNK signaling, retrograde dynein impairment, and NEFH accumulation into a coherent dying-back axonopathy model relevant across ALS genotypes, whereas C05 is well grounded but confined to C9orf72 DPR pathology and its logic is strained by the very RANGAP1 sequestration it posits (activating a sequestered GAP may not restore envelope-localized hydrolysis).

s1: C05 is anchored in the most firmly established GA biology—bisretinoid/lipofuscin accumulation from lysosomal insufficiency—with a textbook MTORC1-TFEB cascade, whereas C08 cGAS-STING-IFNB1-senescence loop is mechanistically deep and coherent but its causal link to geographic lesion progression remains emerging and partly inferential.
s2: C08 offers a more complete causal chain (oxidized mtDNA → cGAS-STING → TBK1/IRF3 → IFNB1-STAT1 → senescence/SASP → RPE dropout) that integrates oxidative stress, innate immunity, and cell-autonomous degeneration, whereas C05 premise that lysosomal biogenesis upregulation can clear chemically refractory bisretinoids like A2E is weaker, and the asserted constitutive MTORC1 activity in GA RPE is not independently justified.

s1: C01 rests on the strongest causal chain in ALS biology—TDP-43 nuclear loss-of-function driving STMN2/UNC13A cryptic exon inclusion, with UNC13A genetically validated by GWAS and STMN2 depletion reproducibly linked to axon degeneration—whereas C06 relies on the more speculative stress-granule-to-solid-aggregate seeding hypothesis and risks on-target toxicity from globally disrupting essential m6A pathways.
s2: C01 is anchored in the most robust causal chain in ALS biology—TDP-43 nuclear depletion driving STMN2 and UNC13A cryptic exon inclusion—with strong support from human genetics (UNC13A GWAS), replicated pathology across ~97% of cases, and direct functional links to axon maintenance and NMJ synaptic transmission; C06's m6A-YTHDF condensate reinforcement loop is mechanistically interesting and biophysically articulate, but the step from METTL3-dependent methylation to pathogenic liquid-to-solid maturation remains largely hypothesized, and chronic METTL3 inhibition carries broad, hard-to-interpret mRNA metabolism confounds.

s1: C02 is anchored in the most common genetic cause of ALS (C9orf72) with DPR-mediated nucleocytoplasmic transport defects among the best-validated toxic pathways, and it targets a convergent upstream node (KPNB1-dependent import) that plausibly renormalizes Ran gradient, GLE1 export, and TDP-43 retention in both familial and sporadic disease; C03 rests on a single, very recent chaperone finding and a rare mutation subset (hnRNPA1 D262V/N), limiting disease breadth and evidential depth.
s2: C02 integrates a well-validated multi-node cascade (C9orf72 DPRs jamming NUP62/RANGAP1, Ran gradient collapse, GLE1-mediated export failure, TDP-43 mislocalization) tied to the most common genetic cause of ALS, whereas C03 rests on a single chaperone-client interaction relevant mainly to rare hnRNPA1-mutation carriers, limiting disease breadth despite its elegant proximal-cause logic.

s1: C09 rests on human genetic evidence with each causal step supported—SPTLC1 gain-of-function variants weaken ORMDL-mediated feedback, driving 1-deoxysphingolipid accumulation that is directly neurotoxic—whereas C04 core MMP9-upregulation finding is solid but its specific LAMB2/COL4A2 cleavage mechanism at the endplate is an untested inference, and MMP9's documented action in motor neuron somata may not be engaged by a peripherally restricted blockade.
s2: C09 rests on direct human genetic causality — SPTLC1 gain-of-function variants cause a juvenile ALS phenotype with a defined biochemical fingerprint (1-deoxysphingolipid neurotoxicity), and the ORMDL axis is the documented endogenous feedback loop that these variants disrupt, making the intervention mechanistically precise; C04 is grounded in solid SOD1 mouse data on MMP9 in vulnerable fast-fatigable motor neurons, but the specific LAMB2/COL4A2 cleavage mechanism is inferential, and peripheral blockade addresses denervation delay rather than neuron death.

s1: C05 engages a genetically and literature-validated upstream hub in C9orf72 ALS—DPR sequestration of KPNB1, Ran-gradient collapse, and nucleoporin/GLE1 disruption—with greater molecular depth, though it overreaches in claiming KPNB1 restoration would rescue FUS import (a TNPO1/Transportin-1 cargo) and mRNA export; C09 Treg–microglia axis is accurate and progression-linked but largely correlative and less specific to the motor-neuron degeneration cascade.
s2: C09 presents a coherent, clinically corroborated causal chain — Treg functional decline as a strong progression correlate, loss of CTLA-4/IL-10/TGF-beta restraint permitting cytotoxic microglial/macrophage activation tracked by CHIT1/YKL40/sCD14 — already validated biologically in ALS patients (IMMODALS). C05 is mechanistically ambitious but contains internal weaknesses: FUS import is largely Transportin-dependent rather than KPNB1-dependent, and overexpressing KPNB1 would titrate DPRs but does not directly rebuild a RanGTP gradient dissipated by nucleoporin damage, making the proposed rescue of TDP-43/FUS localization and GLE1 export partly speculative.

s1: C01 is anchored in exceptionally well-validated disease biology—TDP-43 nuclear depletion in ~97% of ALS cases, with STMN2 and UNC13A cryptic exon inclusion robustly demonstrated in patient spinal cord and iPSC motor neurons, and the strategy of acting downstream of TDP-43 avoids gain-of-toxicity risks; C05 convergence model (KIF5A cargo-binding defects plus TDP-43-mediated Miro1/TRAK2 destabilization) is plausible but more speculative, and the claim that stabilizing RHOT1 can bypass a defective kinesin-cargo interface is mechanistically uncertain and risks impairing PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy and transport-quality-control checkpoints.
s2: C01 rests on the most robustly validated downstream mechanism in ALS—near-universal TDP-43 nuclear loss-of-function driving STMN2/UNC13A cryptic exon inclusion—supported by patient tissue data and risk-variant genetics, whereas C05 convergence model (Miro1 stabilization bypassing KIF5A cargo-binding defects) is coherent but more speculative, and it ignores risks like interference with PINK1/Parkin-mediated Miro1 removal and mitophagy.

s1: C06 offers a precise, linearly testable causal chain (MMP9-mediated CD59 shedding, unopposed C5b-9 assembly, sublytic Ca2+ influx, RPE death) anchored at a validated terminal checkpoint of complement injury while explicitly sparing upstream complement functions, whereas C07 is integrative but rests on a blunter master-regulator overexpression whose link to the specific RPE death pathway in GA is less direct and carries pleiotropy risk from constitutive TFEB.
s2: C06 anchors to the only clinically validated axis in GA—complement—and acts at the terminal CD59/MAC checkpoint where each step (MMP9 shedding, surface CD59 loss, sublytic C5b-9 Ca2+ influx, RPE death) is individually documented and measurable, whereas C07 TFEB hub is elegant systems biology but rests on less-validated causal premises, notably that boosting lysosomal biogenesis can clear chemically degradation-refractory bisretinoids like A2E and that MTORC1 hyperactivity is the true bottleneck in aged RPE.

s1: C04 rests on a causally supported chain with human data — DICER1 loss and Alu RNA accumulation are documented in GA RPE and are sufficient to induce degeneration in vivo, and cGAS/STING-driven IFN signaling plausibly links nucleic-acid sensing to RPE senescence and death; C09 iron/hepcidin axis is plausible and histologically grounded, but the leap from HFE risk polymorphisms to local HAMP-SLC40A1 dysregulation as a driver (rather than epiphenomenon) is more speculative.
s2: C04 builds on directly documented human GA evidence (DICER1 loss, cytosolic Alu RNA/cDNA accumulation) with demonstrated sufficiency to induce RPE degeneration in vivo, and the cGAS-STING-IFNB1 cascade is molecularly coherent including the reverse-transcribed cDNA ligand for MB21D1; C09 is mechanistically layered and chemically precise (HAMP-SLC40A1-Fenton-DNA axis, HFE risk variants, ferritin saturation), but its central causal claim in GA remains more correlative, with internal tension in how HFE polymorphisms map onto local hepcidin upregulation.

s1: C02 traces a precise, cell-autonomous causal chain from the near-universal TDP-43 pathology to disruption of a defined protein-protein interaction (VAPB-RMDN3/PTPIP51), collapse of ITPR1-VDAC1 calcium transfer, and bioenergetic failure, anchored by VAPB's status as a bona fide ALS gene and existing literature on TDP-43-mediated untethering; C09 is mechanistically sound but operates at a broader, more downstream level of general autophagic clearance.
s2: C02 offers a specific, literature-anchored causal chain (TDP-43 binding to RMDN3/PTPIP51 disrupting the VAPB tether, impairing ITPR1-VDAC1 calcium transfer and ATP) tied to the hallmark pathology of ~97% of ALS cases, and engages ALS-relevant genes (VAPB), whereas C09 TFEB/autophagy narrative is coherent but generic across neurodegeneration and its C9orf72-SMCR8 compensation claim is more speculative.

s1: C06 anchors its cascade in established GA risk architecture (CFH/CFB raising intracellular complement load, ARMS2/HTRA1 sensitizing mitochondria), identifies a specific proximal enzymatic node (CTSB-mediated intracellular C3 cleavage, mitochondrial C3b opsonization, OXPHOS collapse), and offers a coherent explanation for why extracellular complement inhibitors like pegcetacoplan only partially slow GA; C08 CNN2–actin–focal adhesion cascade is plausible but rests on a single unverifiable citation (PMID 42685076 appears unassigned/fabricated) and a generic cytoskeleton-upstream-of-everything logic with thinner disease-specific causal evidence.
s2: C06 grounds its cascade in the strongest established AMD genetics (CFH Y402H, ARMS2/HTRA1) and in the well-documented clinical gap that extracellular complement inhibitors only partially slow GA, with each step (CTSB-mediated intracellular C3 cleavage, mitochondrial C3b opsonization, OXPHOS collapse) individually supported by complosome and RPE stress literature; C08 multi-pathway cytoskeletal-focal adhesion model is coherent and physiologically literate, but its entire premise rests on a single unreplicated genetic association for CNN2, making it more speculative despite its breadth.

s1: C01 rests on one of the best-validated causal chains in ALS biology — nuclear TDP-43 loss de-repressing the STMN2 cryptic exon, confirmed in human postmortem tissue and iPSC models, and applicable to ~97% of TDP-43 proteinopathy cases; C04 chain (VCP segregase failure → persistent G3BP1 condensates → irreversible TDP-43/FUS aggregates) involves contested steps, applies to a rare genetic subtype, and carries an internal tension since mutant VCP also impairs autophagic flux itself, so TFEB-driven biogenesis may not resolve the bottleneck.
s2: C01 rests on a rigorously validated causal chain (TDP-43 nuclear loss → STMN2 cryptic splice/polyadenylation → STMN2 depletion → axon degeneration) that applies to ~97% of ALS cases, and it correctly identifies downstream effector restoration as a strategy orthogonal to fixing TDP-43 mislocalization. C04 is broader in scope (VCP–stress granule–aggrephagy–TDP-43/FUS) but carries a mechanistic vulnerability: mutant VCP/p97 is itself required for autophagosome maturation and lysosomal fusion, and VCP-mutant models often show constitutive TFEB activation with impaired flux, so simply amplifying autophagy-lysosomal biogenesis may not bypass the defect and could worsen substrate backlog.

s1: C03 builds a detailed, multi-layer causal chain (GSK3B activation -> VAPB phosphorylation -> tether dissolution -> ITPR3-VDAC1 Ca2+/phospholipid transfer failure -> OXPHOS deficit) that connects familial ALS genetics (VAPB/ALS8) with TDP-43/FUS pathology present in the vast majority of cases, and explicitly addresses selective vulnerability of high-demand motor neurons; C07 chain is credible and upstream but hinges on the debated primacy of nucleocytoplasmic transport blockade and applies only to the C9orf72 subset.
s2: C07 targets the disease-specific upstream lesion in C9orf72 ALS with a well-validated causal chain (repeat RNA and DPRs sequestering KPNB1/NUP62 and impairing nucleocytoplasmic transport), giving it stronger mechanistic directness; C03 VAPB-RMDN3 tether mechanism is plausible and convergent for TDP-43/FUS pathology, but the GSK3B phosphorylation-to-tether-dissolution link is less established and GSK3B pleiotropy weakens causal specificity.

s1: C07 is awarded for mechanistic depth — it integrates DPR toxicity, TDP-43 mislocalization, and nucleocytoplasmic transport failure into a self-amplifying convergent loop supported by consistent observations across familial and sporadic ALS, positioning the Ran gradient as an upstream hub; C09 is coherent and benefits from in vivo genetic validation (Nlrp3/Casp1 deletion in SOD1G93A), but it is a generic neuroinflammatory cascade downstream of the primary neuronal pathology and largely SOD1-model-anchored.
s2: C09 presents a causally-anchored cascade with genetic loss-of-function evidence (Nlrp3/Casp1 deletion in SOD1G93A mice) and clear upstream-node logic, whereas C07 convergent nucleocytoplasmic-transport hub is well-documented but its intervention rationale is conceptually weaker, since enhancing RCC1 GEF activity cannot sustain a Ran gradient if NPC permeability and RANGAP1/NUP62 localization remain disrupted, and 're-stabilizing' nucleoporins lacks a defined mechanism.

s1: C05 engages the most prevalent ALS pathology (TDP-43 mislocalization, present in ~97% of cases) and links it mechanistically to a defined lethal cascade (nuclear depletion → defective HDAC1/RNF168/XRCC1-mediated repair → persistent DNA damage → p53-dependent degeneration), with each link supported by published work on FUS/TDP-43 in DDR; C07 PINK1/PRKN–OPTN/TBK1 mitophagy logic is canonical and genetically anchored (OPTN, TBK1 are ALS genes), but boosting ubiquitin tags via USP30 may not fix downstream autophagy-execution defects, and neuronal mitophagy dependence on Parkin is contested.
s2: C05 engages the dominant ALS pathology (TDP-43/FUS mislocalization, present in ~97% of cases) via a proximal loss-of-function mechanism with documented links to impaired DNA repair and p53-dependent degeneration, whereas C07 mitophagy narrative, although anchored by bona fide ALS genes OPTN/TBK1, is a more generic stress-response deficit that is correlative across many neurodegenerative contexts.

s1: C09 integrates the full ferroptotic execution circuit (NCOA4/TFRC-driven labile iron, ACSL4-dependent PUFA-PE loading, GPX4/SLC7A11 decline) and proposes a coherent two-point collapse of the death module with explicit attention to RPE lipid-peroxidation evidence in GA, whereas C10 rests on a clean but simpler iron-flux argument whose aceruloplasminemia anchor only partially maps onto GA and glosses over the retina's need for TFRC-supplied iron; C09 mechanistic granularity wins, though both cite genuine histopathology.
s2: C10 targets the most upstream, genetically validated node—CP/SLC40A1 efflux failure with persistent import is anchored by human aceruloplasminemia retinopathy and documented iron overload in GA tissue, giving causal disease grounding that C09 downstream execution-module framing lacks.

s1: C01 is anchored to the near-universal TDP-43 pathology with strong human validation—cryptic exon insertion in STMN2 and UNC13A is robustly observed in ALS spinal cord and iPSC motor neurons, and UNC13A is a genetically confirmed ALS/FTD risk locus whose risk variants enhance cryptic splicing—whereas C08 causal chain (SIGMAR1 loss destabilizing the VAPB-PTPIP51 tether driving Ca2+ overload and mPTP opening) rests on a rare juvenile-ALS mutation and model data that is not clearly linked to the common disease mechanism.
s2: C01 is anchored to the near-universal TDP-43 pathology (~97% of ALS) with a causally validated chain (cryptic exon insertion → NMD → STMN2/UNC13A depletion) supported by human genetics (UNC13A risk variants), postmortem tissue, and iPSC data, whereas C08 builds on a rare juvenile ALS gene and contains an internal tension (uncoupling ER-to-MCU uptake should reduce, not overload, mitochondrial Ca2+), making its death-pathway logic less coherent and more speculative.

s1: C07 edges out because its causal chain has direct experimental support—RNASEH1 overexpression demonstrably rescues FUS-mutant toxicity, DNA damage is documented in human ALS tissue, and SETX-linked ALS4 genetically anchors R-loop/repair pathology—whereas C04 terminal link (mitophagy-derived ROS driving pTDP-43 phosphorylation/truncation) is plausible but indirect, and pure mitophagy failure (PINK1/PRKN-null states, mitophagy-deficient Optn mice) causes Parkinson's or no neurodegeneration rather than ALS, weakening causality. C04 genetic anchor (TBK1/OPTN) is genuine but complicated by incomplete penetrance and TBK1's pleiotropic immune/autophagy roles.
s2: Both mechanisms are coherent and anchored in ALS biology, but C07 ties the near-universal hallmark of FUS/TDP-43 cytoplasmic mislocalization to a specific, well-documented nuclear loss-of-function (R-loop accumulation, PARP1-XRCC1 repair collapse, p53-dependent neuronal death), with independent genetic support from SETX/ALS4; C04 genetic anchor via TBK1/OPTN is strong, but the downstream ROS-to-phospho-TDP-43 causal chain is more correlative and PRKN defects are only rare contributors.
